title: A Brave New World: A Quantitative Model of A Self-Sufficient Martian Society

context_sources.name: Smith, McPherson and Smith-Lovin, social distance and homophily
Pew Research Center, April 2012 Values Survey
Pingali and Evenson, Handbook of Agricultural Economics
National Center for Health Statistics, birth and death rates

limitations: The dimensional chain for the farmer count is flattened, though 2,401.41 and 2,448.54 are legible.
The food-demand sum is broken across lines and reconstructed from the prose.
The dissimilarity formula is printed with its indices detached.
The happiness index is printed with its subscripts scattered.
The two schooling fits are reported only by R-squared and AIC, not by coefficients.

tasks: Define metrics for income, education and equality
Choose the age, gender and occupation mix of the first 10,000 settlers
Link schooling to GDP and set the years of education
Design a wage structure and compute GDP and the Gini coefficient
Model racial segregation and gender policy
Merge the three models into a happiness index
Test three migration policies and an evacuation bound

section_map.summary: Three priorities, a quarter farmers, a tiny Gini coefficient.
Income split into efficiency and equality; dissimilarity for segregation.
A quasi-Markov chain, a birth scalar of 1.08, 4,000 young and 6,000 working.
2,449 farmers by dimensional analysis, health scaled by traveler illness.
Two tied fits, 11.02 years, GDP of 289.6 million.
Three salary tiers, GDP 288.7 million, Gini 0.0336.
Homophily at 1.2; tiered pay cuts dissimilarity.
Four proxies, survey weights, equal pay loses.
Three scenarios; gradual inflow is best; 8,304 in an evacuation.
A letter of recommendations to the agency.

contributions.summary: A birth scalar chosen so the population grows and then stabilizes.
Two independent models agreeing on GDP to under one percent.
A tradeoff between two equalities settled by recomputing one index.

dependency_graph.handoff: The stable population and the working-age count size the schooling pipeline
The schooling projection gives the GDP the income model is checked against
The tiered salaries are what pull movers away from their own group
Dissimilarity, the Gini coefficient, GDP and years of schooling become the four proxies

assumptions.summary: No trade, plentiful land, Earth vital rates, and monogamous families.
Family size and gender are the same in every occupation.
A shared new identity reduces racial bias.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: US fertility and mortality over the last decade, capped at age 100.
Barro-Lee years of schooling joined to World Bank GDP per capita.
Pew Values Survey answers scored 3, 2, 1, 0 and normalized.

models.summary: A quasi-Markov age chain and an occupation sizing.
Two tied fits from schooling to GDP per person.
Three wage tiers inside the output identity.
A segregation chain driven by homophily and pay.
A four-term happiness index with survey weights.

verification.summary: The income GDP of 288.732 million matches the education GDP of 289.613 million.
Flattening wages lowers the happiness index for all seven subgroups.

results_trace.summary: Gini coefficient 0.0335591, tax rate 73.64 percent, GDP per capita at the 76th percentile.

writing_logic.summary: A published claim is simulated and rejected before the chosen mix is given.
Equal pay is shown to fail before tiered pay is adopted.
The tradeoff is resolved by recomputing the index, not by argument.

language_observations.summary: A headcount is built by chaining units in one line.
Two fits tie, so both are kept to bound a range.
The harmonic mean is justified by one sentence: one right does not cancel one wrong.
Each recommendation names the number and the objection it answers.

visualization_observations.summary: Figure 1: age mix over time with no children at the start.
Figure 2: age mix over time for the chosen starting population.
Scatter of happiness against the youth unemployment rate.
GDP per capita against years of schooling, with two fits.
Lorenz curve of the colony against the line of perfect equality.
Figure 3: dissimilarity over time when all tiers pay the same.
Figure 4: dissimilarity over time under tiered pay.
Table 1: scores of 3, 2, 1 and 0 for survey answers.
Table 2: priority weights and happiness by income tier.
Table 3: priority weights by gender and by working versus retired.
Table 4: happiness before and after equalizing wages.
Population over time after a one-time migration.
Population over time under gradual migration.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: Both schooling fits explain little, yet the projection is used as a point.
Earth income slices are treated as the colony's occupational tiers.
Traveler illness rates on Earth scale the whole health workforce.

weaknesses.summary: The schooling fits have an R-squared of 0.27 and no printed coefficients.
The homophily factor and the move rate are chosen, not estimated, with no sensitivity run.
Fertility, mortality and the census all come from one country on Earth.

independent_extensions.summary: Sweep the homophily factor and the move rate.
Report the coefficients and try a fit that beats R-squared 0.27.
Model the unemployment the sudden inflow creates.

candidate_rule_impacts.summary: Keep services public and goods private, with pay rising by skill.
Cap unplanned migration by the minimum public spend per person.

unresolved_questions.question: What coefficients did the two schooling fits return?
How sensitive is dissimilarity to the homophily factor?
How many jobs appear in the years after a sudden inflow?
